Cell. The cell is the smallest unit of life capable of independent existence and reproduction. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells, which arise only from pre-existing cells. Cells are bounded by a cell membrane that controls what enters and exits. They contain DNA as their genetic material and machinery for energy production, protein synthesis, and growth. Two major types exist: prokaryotic cells, which are bacteria and archaea and lack a nucleus, and eukaryotic cells, which are animals, plants, and fungi that compartmentalize functions into specialized organelles.

All cells are bounded by a cell membrane, or plasma membrane, which is a lipid bilayer with embedded and peripheral proteins that controls transport and signaling. All cells contain cytoplasm, a gel-like matrix containing water, salts, proteins, and organelles. All cells contain DNA as their hereditary material. DNA is replicated and passed to daughter cells during cell division. All cells carry out metabolism—chemical reactions that extract energy from nutrients and build cellular components. All cells synthesize proteins via ribosomes, using the genetic code to translate DNA instructions.

Prokaryotic cells are small, ranging from one to ten micrometers across, with no nucleus. DNA is a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid region, not enclosed by a membrane. They lack membrane-bound organelles; instead, metabolic functions occur in the cytoplasm or attached to the cell membrane. Prokaryotes can divide rapidly—every twenty minutes under optimal conditions—via binary fission, which is asexual reproduction. They are surrounded by a rigid cell wall, made of peptidoglycan in bacteria, that provides structural support.

Eukaryotic cells are larger, ranging from ten to one hundred micrometers, with a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope. DNA is organized into linear chromosomes. They contain membrane-bound organelles, each with specialized functions. Mitochondria produce energy. The endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes proteins and lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules. Lysosomes digest material. Chloroplasts, found in plants, perform photosynthesis.

Eukaryotes divide more slowly—typically once per twenty-four hours—but allow sexual reproduction, which enables genetic recombination. They possess a cytoskeleton, networks of protein filaments that provide structure, enable movement, and facilitate transport within the cell.

Cells grow and divide in a coordinated process called the cell cycle. G1 phase is a gap during growth. S phase is when DNA synthesis occurs. G2 phase is another gap during preparation. M phase is mitosis, when division occurs. During S phase, DNA replication is semiconservative. Checkpoint controls ensure replication is complete and accurate before division proceeds. The cell cycle is regulated by checkpoint proteins, including p53, known as the guardian of the genome. These proteins detect errors and halt the cycle or trigger cell death if damage is irreparable.

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, essential for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. Meiosis produces four haploid gametes—sperm and egg cells—with half the chromosome number. This is essential for sexual reproduction and genetic diversity. Binary fission in prokaryotes is rapid and asexual.

In multicellular organisms, different cell types—nerve cells, muscle cells, immune cells—express different sets of genes, resulting in specialized functions and structures. Differentiation is the process by which a generic cell becomes specialized. It is largely irreversible and driven by transcription factors and epigenetic modifications. Specialized cells lose the ability to divide, such as neurons, or divide infrequently, such as muscle cells.
